ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Myeloid progenitors are stem cells in the bone marrow that give rise to all mature myeloid cells. Their dysfunction leads to cytopenias or clonal disorders. Clinicians assess lineage distribution, marrow morphology, and molecular markers to guide diagnosis and treatment.

sections.p: Myeloid progenitors (CMP) are bipotent cells that differentiate into granulocyte, monocyte, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lineages. Diagnosis requires bone marrow aspirate with cytology, flow cytometry for lineage markers, and cytogenetics for clonal abnormalities.
b: CMP expresses CD34+, CD38+, CD123+, CD45low

t.b: Shows neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia; indicates lineage loss or excess
Assesses cellularity, dysplasia, blast percentage; >20% blasts suggests acute myeloid leukemia
Detects abnormal immunophenotype; e.g., loss of CD45, aberrant CD7
Identifies translocations (e.g., t(8;21), inv(16)) or mutations (FLT3, NPM1)

sections.p: Staging follows WHO AML criteria: normal karyotype, favorable, intermediate, adverse. Severity is gauged by blast count, cytopenias, organ dysfunction, and molecular risk.

t.b: Determines AML vs. MDS; higher blasts correlate with poorer prognosis

sections.p: Acute changes stem from infections, chemotherapy, radiation, or inherited syndromes. Chronic cytopenias often arise from nutritional deficiencies, HIV, TB, malaria, or autoimmune marrow suppression.

t.b: High in iron overload; low in deficiency

sections.p: Patients may have fatigue, infections, bruising, or bleeding. In acute leukemia, fever, weight loss, night sweats, and organomegaly are common.
A stepwise approach starts with CBC, then marrow aspirate, flow cytometry, and cytogenetics. In low-resource settings, peripheral smear and basic chemistry can guide initial management.

t.b: Detects cytopenias and blast cells; abnormal ratios suggest lineage skewing
Identifies dysplasia, blasts, and ring sideroblasts; guides urgency
Confirms diagnosis, blast percentage, and morphology
Differentiates myeloid from lymphoid blasts and identifies aberrant markers
Provides prognostic information and therapeutic targets

sections.p: Rapidly rising blasts, uncontrolled bleeding, severe infections, or organ failure require urgent referral. Complications include tumor lysis syndrome, marrow failure, and secondary malignancies.

Treat underlying cause first. For AML, induction chemotherapy with cytarabine and an anthracycline is standard; supportive care includes transfusions, antibiotics, and infection prophylaxis. In MDS, erythropoietin or lenalidomide for anemia; hypomethylating agents for higher risk.
b: Allogeneic stem cell transplant for eligible patients

t.b: Blocks DNA synthesis; effective in AML blasts
Inhibits DNA methyltransferase; improves survival in high-risk MDS

sections.p: Regular CBCs, marrow exams, and monitoring for relapse are essential. Prevention focuses on infection control, nutritional support, and avoiding myelotoxic drugs when possible.
b: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics that cause marrow suppression

sections.p: Myelodysplastic syndromes mimic chronic cytopenias; acute lymphoblastic leukemia can present with similar blasts. Chronic myeloid leukemia shows a different blast threshold and BCR-ABL translocation.
Low blast counts may be missed in peripheral smear; iron deficiency can mask anemia severity; marrow fibrosis can reduce aspirate yield.
b: Low peripheral blasts despite high marrow blasts

faq.q: What is the most common cause of myeloid progenitor failure in low-resource settings?
faq.a: Infections such as HIV, TB, and malaria, plus nutritional deficiencies like iron, B12, and folate.

faq.q: Can a patient with myeloid progenitor disease be treated without a bone marrow biopsy?
faq.a: Initial clues come from CBC and peripheral smear, but definitive diagnosis and risk stratification require marrow examination.

faq.q: Why is cytarabine used in AML treatment?
faq.a: It blocks DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing myeloid blasts, leading to cell death.
